Q: Apply aero glass blur to a specific control area in WPF A:

Unfortunately, there is no method by which you can enable a blur-behind effect on a standard wpf control. However, some controls (popups, menus, and other windows) are technically rendered inside other windows. You can retrieve the Handle to the underlying window and pass that to a DWM function. Another tricky method is to host native controls in a HwndHost. However, this causes its own issues. HwndHost only supports native content, meaning you can’t just drop a wpf control inside. Your best option for bluring a specific portion of your window is to create a new window, set the start position to manual, set top and left to specific points relative to the main window, and set up logic such that the new window moves and resizes with the main window. All you’d have to do then is apply whatever dwm or composition effect you want on the new window. This usually isn’t practical, especially if you want that piece of your main window to be constantly blurred, and even more so if your app can be dragged and resized.

Q: An "additionalProperties: type: string" prevents openapi-to-rust tool from generating a REST Server A:

openapi-to-rust tool looks not working for this case.

I've managed to generate a REST server through OpenAPI generator version 7.24.0 (not lower) using its rust-salvo generator. (not rust-server or rust-axum ones that are also not working, but for others reasons than in the question)

Q: Cannot open Gemini in Colab A:

Yes, language might be the problem here. Try setting your Google account language to English, then open Colab as
https://colab.research.google.com/?hl=en and reload.

Next, test in an incognito window with extensions disabled and third-party cookies allowed, since ad blockers and Safari or Brave's default cookie blocking break the AI panel. Also make sure a birthday is actually set on the account, a missing one gets treated as under 18 and it wont work.

If you are in mainland China or Hong Kong, Google's AI endpoints aren't reachable at all from those places, so the panel loads but every request dies, VPN fixes the network side but not the account's registered country.

Finally, If you are using a free tier, its AI usage has monthly limits, and hitting them can show the same generic error.

To tell which category you are in, run from google.colab import ai; print(ai.generate_text("hi")) in a cell. If it works, the problem is your browser or session; if it errors too, its account or region, and settings changes won't fix it.

Q: Calling PHP's mdate() emits: "Warning: It is not safe to rely on the system's timezone settings." A:

I guess you have php 5.3. Anyway , the solution is to define the timezone to php by adding to your php files the next code before using any time/date function:

date_default_timezone_set('UTC');

or , a better solution , editing your php.ini file and adding:

date.timezone = "America/Anchorage"

America/Anchorage is the timezone , use the one that is relevant to you from the list:

https://www.php.net/manual/en/timezones.php

Q: GCC vs MS C++ Compiler A:

There are pros and cons with all tools. Those that are the most used are the less problematics so what you need is a list of differences between the two compilers (are they are known to not be harmful). You can find some on stackoverflow or somewhere else.

EDIT: things are changing all the time so just keep searching at the time you discover this answer. For example, today Clang have become a very good compiler alternative for a lot of companies. MSVC is updating featurres faster than before at this time.

From what I know (around 2010):

  • GCC is cross-platfom : all unix-like platform have a version, and even others. MSVC is Microsoft-OS targets only;
  • GCC is known to implement (a bit) more correctly the C++ standard. It also currently implement more features of the next standard than other compilers;
  • MSVC is better on compilation time and generate faster code than GCC (from several discussions on the boost mailing list);
  • MSVC goes with a free IDE (Visual Studio Express) that is known to have a really powerful debugger, that makes debugging sessions (70% of programming time) easier. GCC don't realy have an equivalent, althought GDB seems to be something similar (I don't know much about it).
  • At this time, GCC integrate far more C++11 language features than MSVC, almost the complete upgrade. MSVC only integrate a few, importants, but still not a lot. If you want to do something cross-platform using both these compilers, you'll have to limit your C++11 use to MSVC subset.
  • (in the beta version of MSVC) MSVC integrate the whole new C++11 standard library while GCC C++11 standard library is far from being complete. Again, if you want to use both compilers, check the common subsets.

Now there are a lot other differences, but I think those are the main to know to make an idea. If you're targetting cross-platform dev, maybe using GCC will be more helpful, maybe not as MSVC seem better on windows than the GCC port (MinGW).

When there is a blurry line between too widely used tool, it's always because those tools just solve problems in the same domain differently, so just list the differences and make your choice on a project basis.
